newsitem.title: USA: U.S. does not want to corner N.Korea, admiral says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. does not want to corner N.Korea, admiral says.

text.p: The commander of U.S. forces in the Pacific said on Monday the United States does not want to corner North Korea, which could risk a sudden military strike that would wreak havoc in South Korea.
"We are in the business of trying not to corner them so much so that they would feel called upon to lash out," Adm. Joseph Prueher, commander of the U.S. Pacific Command, said.

He told reporters North Korea would not be able to invade and hold the South but it has 700 missile launchers and artillery that could "wreak a lot of havoc and take a lot of lives if a conflict should erupt there."

He said he believed the United States and its allies should continue to send food to famine-stricken North Korea both for humanitarian reasons and to help prevent a government collapse or implosion that could be violent.

Asked about the possibility that a collapse in Pyongyang could send waves of refugees across borders, possibly with soldiers shooting refugees as they fled, Prueher said allies should try to avoid a collapse that could bring such violence.
"I think that would be the smartest thing for us to do there and I think that's pretty much the track we're on."

North Korea was supposed to meet with U.S. officials in New York on Wednesday on a U.S.-South Korea proposal for peace talks among those three countries and China, but last week it postponed the meeting for the second time.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said it was uncertain when the meeting would be held. "Having postponed it once and set a date, I don't think we're in a position where we want to set a date again," he told a news briefing.
North Korean officials have said that before holding the meeting they want to conclude talks with U.S. grain firm Cargill Inc. on a barter deal for 500,000 metric tons of wheat.
U.S. officials insisted that Washington did not plan to intervene in the grain talks, for example by helping to finance North Korea's purchase.

The North Koreans "are obviously trying to link and leverage here," one official said. "We're not willing to play the game. They think we're so desperate to get this meeting, that maybe we'll put some money in the pot, and frankly we don't think that's necessary."
Burns, however, held out the possibility that Washington might separately send food aid to North Korea, as it has done in the past.

He said Washington understood that the U.N. World Food Programme was considering making another emergency appeal for North Korea, and that if it did so, "the United States will consider it very seriously".
South Korea's Red Cross, meanwhile, said it would send 700 metric tons of flour to the North on Tuesday, in addition to 300 tons shipped on Friday, a spokesman said.

In a move apparently aimed at putting pressure on the United States, North Korea said on Monday it has only half the grain it needs to feed its people because of two years of floods that destroyed crops.
